language_wrapper: Let P(x) and Q(x) be distinct real polynomials of degree {degree_n} whose coefficients of x^0, x^1, ..., x^{degree_n} are all nonzero. Let r be the total multiplicity of their common real roots, and let s be the number of indices j in {0,1,...,{degree_n}} for which the coefficient of x^j in P equals the coefficient of x^j in Q. Determine the maximum possible value of r + s.
hardness_rationale: Compared with the seed, this family explicitly defines s as the count of exactly equal coefficients and requires maximizing r+s under the constraint that both polynomials are dense (all coefficients nonzero). The solution demands combining fewnomial bounds via Descartes' rule of signs on P−Q, careful treatment of multiplicities, and an additional parity obstruction (r cannot reach n because that would force Q to be a scalar multiple of P). The optimizer must navigate a piecewise-linear trade-off between sparsity of P−Q and the impossibility of sharing all n real roots. This yields a closed-form answer dependent on the parity of n, adding subtlety and complexity beyond the original problem.
notes: Key steps: (1) Any common real root of P and Q is a real root of T=P−Q; (2) If both polynomials have nonzero constant terms, 0 is not a common root; (3) A k-term polynomial has <= k−1 positive and <= k−1 negative real roots, so T has <= 2(n−s) nonzero real roots; (4) r cannot be n because that would imply P and Q are scalar multiples. Optimizing min(n−1, 2(n−s)) + s over integer s gives the stated formula. Instances with large n are chosen to avoid trivial guessing and ensure a substantial optimization step.
source_question: Let \(P(x),Q(x)\) be distinct 4046-degree real polynomials with non-zero coefficients. Let \(r\) be the number of their common real roots (multiplicity counted) and \(s\) be the number of their common terms. Find the maximum possible value of \(r + s\).
